A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OV-MER work and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Relocated and renumbered material can be reliably matched.

before.justification: v2 reports original MLLM benchmark results, modality and prompting analyses, dataset analyses, and a user study reporting 97.5% preference for OV-MERD labels' informativeness.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds discriminative-model evaluations, inter-annotator agreement results, and a human-perception alignment study.

M1.justification: Sections 2–4 retain the human-LLM annotation pipeline, CLUE variants, label extraction, and S2 inference strategy. Added annotation disclosures and implementations of comparison methods do not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

E1.justification: Appendix U newly uses IEMOCAP and MELD to train discriminative models evaluated on OV-MERD. These datasets were previously described as related datasets, rather than used in reported experiments. This adds substantial source-dataset and cross-dataset transfer coverage; OV-MERD itself remains unchanged.

E2.justification: v3 Table 15 adds eight evaluated discriminative comparators: MFM, MISA, GMFN, MFN, MulT, LMF, TFN, and Attention, each trained on MELD or IEMOCAP and compared with MLLMs. The original Table 2 comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: v3 introduces training on IEMOCAP/MELD followed by testing on OV-MERD, using specified visual, acoustic, and lexical feature extractors. Section 5 also adds a nine-annotator, 20-sample binary alignment study with incorrect-label inspection controls. The original benchmark protocol remains unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds substantive annotation-quality validation: direct human-perception alignment testing and pairwise agreement analysis for both annotation rounds in Appendix L. Appendix S additionally analyzes cross-language correlations over Table 2. Existing modality, prompting, description-length, and metric-comparison analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix L newly reports inter-annotator reliability estimates using sample-averaged pairwise Jaccard similarity. Both versions already specify two experimental repetitions and report means and standard deviations; v3 does not establish an increase in repetitions or introduce confidence intervals or significance testing.

E6.justification: v3 adds 16 discriminative-model result rows in Table 15, 96% approval in the new perception study, and agreement scores ranging from 0.46–0.57 in round one and 0.64–0.77 in round two. The retained benchmark, ablation, one-hot-label, emotion-wheel, and matching-metric tables are numerically unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix L adds a sample-averaged pairwise agreement definition in Equation 5, and Appendix U formally specifies the Attention comparator through Equations 8–11. Existing emotion-grouping and set-based evaluation definitions remain unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same central claims: open-vocabulary MER, human-LLM dataset construction, suitable evaluation metrics, and a challenging MLLM benchmark. Additional evidence supports these claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations concerning audio resolving textual ambiguity, fine-grained grouping explaining metric correlations, and annotation checks improving reliability. Appendix B discusses acted-data versus real-life domain gaps, while the expanded Impact Statements specify sensitive applications where the dataset should not be used.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code/data repository pointer, the default 7B MLLM size, a 12-sample annotator screening test, source-dataset segmentation/filtering details, and feature extractors and equations for the new Attention comparison. It also documents additional use restrictions. These disclosures do not establish changes to retained experiments.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting the new discriminative comparisons, including MISA, MFM, MFN, and LMF, plus Brown et al. on GPT capabilities. Appendix D's overall positioning and the claim of introducing open-vocabulary MER remain substantially unchanged; publication-metadata updates do not add distinct works.

P1.justification: v3 makes targeted paragraph revisions, clarifies terminology and benchmark roles, reorders metric discussions, and expands appendix headings and impact statements. Most existing prose and the main narrative structure remain recognizable, despite extensive visual reformatting.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column formatting, with widespread resizing and relocation of figures and tables. v3 promotes v2's full appendix emotion-wheel table into main Table 3, swaps Figures 4 and 5, and adds agreement, cross-language correlation, and discriminative-comparison tables.

improvement.justification: Compared with v2's informativeness study and existing benchmark analyses, v3 adds direct label-alignment evidence, quantified annotator agreement, and traditional-model comparisons. These strengthen validation and comparison breadth, while additional access and implementation information improves reproducibility. The 20-sample alignment study and cross-dataset, fixed-label comparator setup limit the strength of the new evidence, supporting a modest overall improvement.
